name: Learning Design & Technology
hook: Build the learning object, then audit it for accessibility before anyone sees it.

make.body: A tactile manipulative for a concept students currently teach with a diagram. The design constraint that makes this a real assignment: it has to work for a learner who cannot see the diagram.

build.body: A working interactive module built in one sitting, then run against an accessibility checklist. The audit is where the learning is. Most AI-generated interfaces fail keyboard navigation and contrast on the first pass, and finding that is the skill.

plan.txt: Choose one concept and write the learning objective before touching a tool. Objective gets peer-reviewed for measurability.
Build the digital module with AI. Ship a rough version fast.
Accessibility audit against WCAG basics: keyboard only, contrast, screen reader, reduced motion. Document every failure and fix it. Submit fabrication file for the tactile version.
User test both versions with three learners outside the class. Revise once. The revision log is the deliverable.

prompt: Build a single self-contained HTML page that teaches this concept interactively: [concept]. The learner is [describe them]. Requirements: it must be fully operable by keyboard alone, meet WCAG AA contrast, respect prefers-reduced-motion, and work on a phone. After you build it, list every accessibility decision you made and every place you are uncertain whether it passes.
tryTuesday: 90 minutes. Minutes 0–15: students write one measurable learning objective for a concept they teach. Minutes 15–45: they generate an interactive module with the accessibility-constrained prompt. Minutes 45–90: they run the embedded a11y-audit demo (or a manual checklist) against their module, documenting every failure — keyboard traps, contrast below 4.5:1, motion that ignores the reduced-motion setting — and fixing what they can in the room. The deliverable is the audit log: what the AI shipped broken and what the student caught, which is where the professional skill lives.

replaces.assignment: The instructional-design project submitted as a storyboard or static prototype.
replaces.lost: The full ADDIE-style documentation and storyboard fidelity.
replaces.gained: Students confront a working artifact and its real accessibility failures instead of a diagram of one; the grade rewards catching what AI generation breaks, which storyboards never expose.

aiFailsHere: AI-generated interfaces look polished and fail the basics: div-based click handlers with no keyboard operability, color choices below WCAG contrast, and animations that ignore prefers-reduced-motion — and the model will assure you it 'meets WCAG AA' without having tested anything. That confident accessibility claim, unbacked by a real audit, is the specific failure a learning designer must learn to distrust.

rubric.description: The learning objective states an observable, assessable behavior.
Keyboard, contrast, screen-reader, and reduced-motion are each checked and results recorded, not assumed.
Each failure is explained in terms of the learner it excludes, not just the rule it breaks.
Fixes actually resolve the flagged failures on re-test.

budget.perStudentCost: $0 for the Tuesday version; roughly $5–12 per student in print or cut stock for a tactile manipulative in the four-week build.
budget.fileDueWeek: Week 3 — fabrication file due after the accessibility audit.
budget.calendarNote: The digital build and audit need no lead time; the tactile version depends on the 7–10 day turnaround, timed for week-4 user testing.

scales.oneSession: The 90-minute build-then-audit session producing an audit log; no fabrication.
scales.fourWeeks: The seeded four-week plan: peer-reviewed objective, fast AI module, accessibility audit and fabrication file, then user testing both versions with outside learners.
scales.oneSemester: A full design cycle — objective, AI-built module, iterated accessibility audits, a fabricated tactile version usable by a learner who cannot see the diagram, and user testing with three outside learners.

promptOutput.model: Claude (Anthropic) — captured 2026-07-27 in an isolated fresh session with no build context; output is unedited.
promptOutput.promptFilled: Filled in as an interactive page teaching how a bill becomes a law in the Hawaiʻi State Legislature, for a high-school civics student, with keyboard, WCAG AA, reduced-motion, and phone requirements.

annotations.marker: Genuinely accessible build: native buttons, aria-current, focus management
annotations.note: Unusually strong — the model used real semantic controls and roving arrow-key navigation rather than div-click handlers, so much of the keyboard story actually works.

annotations.marker: Honest uncertainty: 'I have not run a contrast checker... should be verified'
annotations.note: It flagged the exact claims it could not stand behind — the audit-first mindset the assignment teaches, modeled by the tool itself.
These are the values a student must run through a checker; the a11y-audit demo exists precisely to catch a claim like 'both exceed 4.5:1' stated without measurement.

annotations.marker: Untested touch-target size against the 44px guideline
annotations.note: Named as unmeasured — a real failure mode on phones the student should verify on a device.

related.reason: Both have the student build an AI interactive explainer and then be graded on evaluating it — for accessibility here, for lay comprehension there.
Both generate learning materials fast with AI and make the assessment the critique of what the generator got subtly wrong for real learners.
